siteName.label: Site name
siteName.hint: What visitors see. Any name works.

projectId.label: Web address / Firebase project id
projectId.hint: Becomes <id>.web.app and can NEVER be changed. 6-30 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, starting with a letter.

ownerEmail.label: Your Google email (the owner)
ownerEmail.hint: This verified Google account becomes admin automatically on first sign-in.

steps.title: Create a Google account
steps.why: Used for Firebase and for signing in.
do: Open the [Google sign-up page](https://accounts.google.com/signup).
Enter your name, a username and a password, then finish verification.
steps.success: your name or initial in the top corner.

explainer.title: Why a Google account?
explainer.intro: Firebase, where your site will live, belongs to Google, so you sign in to it with a Google account. Visitors can sign in to your site with Google too, and the account you use here becomes the site's **owner** (its admin). Any Gmail address works.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: It's free, and you only need one.
Use the **same email** for Google, GitHub and Claude, so you never wonder which is which.
Turn on two-step verification: this account controls your website.

terms.meaning: The Google account whose email you enter next. The first time it signs in to your site, it becomes the site's admin, so only you can edit it.
Any @gmail.com address counts as a Google account.

steps.title: Create a GitHub account
steps.why: GitHub keeps your site's files and their history.
do: Open the [GitHub sign-up page](https://github.com/signup).
Enter your email, a password and a username.
Solve the puzzle and type the code GitHub emails you.
Skip any “personalize” questions.

explainer.title: What is GitHub?
explainer.intro: GitHub is a website that keeps your site's files in one place, called a **repository**, and remembers every change ever made to them, like version history for a whole website. Claude edits those files there, and GitHub builds and publishes your site.

sections.heading: How a change travels
points: You tell Claude what you want, in plain words, like “make the title bigger”.

Claude makes the change on a **branch**: a separate copy of your repository, so your live site is untouched while it works. Then it **pushes** (uploads) the branch to GitHub, so the change is saved there.
Claude opens a **pull request**: a request on GitHub that says “please add this change to the live site”. It shows exactly what changed.
As soon as the pull request exists, GitHub automatically builds a private **preview**: a temporary copy of your site with the change in it, at a link only you have.
You open the preview on your phone. Want something different? Tell Claude, and it updates the same pull request and preview.
Happy? Say **ship it**. Claude **merges** the pull request, which adds the change to `main`, the branch your live site comes from. Your site updates within a minute.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: Your repository is **private**: only you can see the files. The website itself is public.
Every change is saved, so a mistake can always be undone.
It's free for what we're doing.

terms.meaning: Your website's folder on GitHub. It holds every file of your site; one repo is one website.
A saved checkpoint with a short note, like “made the title bigger”. You can go back to any commit.
A separate copy of your repo for trying changes without touching the live site. `main` is the branch your live site comes from; `dev` is where new work starts.
Send changes from where Claude works up to your repo on GitHub, so they're saved there.
Bring the latest changes down from GitHub to where you're working.
A request on GitHub to add one branch's changes to another, usually `main`. It shows what changed and gets its own preview link.
A private, temporary copy of your site with the change in it. GitHub builds one for every pull request.
Add the changes from one branch into another. Merging a pull request into `main` puts the change on your live site.
Our word for merging into `main` so the change goes live. You just say “ship it”.

steps.title: Get a paid Claude plan
steps.why: Claude Code isn't on the free plan.
do: Install the Claude app or open [claude.ai](https://claude.ai), and sign up.
On the free plan? Open your profile and tap **Upgrade**.
Choose **Pro** or higher and add payment details.

trouble.fix: Update the app, or use claude.ai/code in your browser.

explainer.title: What is Claude Code?
explainer.intro: Claude is the AI that builds your site with you. **Claude Code** is the part that works on your files in GitHub: you describe what you want in plain words, and it makes the change. It comes with a paid plan (Pro or higher).

sections.heading: Who does what
points: **Claude** writes the code, saves the changes, opens pull requests and builds previews.
**You** decide what you want, look at previews, say **ship it**, and do the few steps that need your own accounts.
Claude never needs your passwords or keys. Don't paste secrets into the chat.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: This is the only paid part. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max or Team plan; see claude.ai for current prices.
Next you'll connect Claude to your GitHub account, so it can work on your repository.

terms.meaning: Where Claude works on your repo, inside the Claude app.
A set of instructions Claude follows. The new-website skill guides you through building a site, one step at a time.
Pro, Max or a Team seat. Claude Code isn't on the free plan.
Any message you send Claude. Plain words work, like “make the heading bigger”.

steps.title: Accept Firebase's terms
steps.why: Accepting now avoids a confusing error later.
do: Signed in to Google, open the Firebase console.
If a terms screen appears, accept it. Don't create a project yet.

explainer.title: What is Firebase?
explainer.intro: Firebase is Google's free toolbox for websites. It puts your site online at its own web address, stores data, and handles sign-in. Each website you make is one Firebase **project**.

callout.label: Your web address
callout.note: When you create a project you choose its **project ID**. That ID becomes your website's address, like `bakery-demo.web.app`. It can never be changed, so choose carefully.

sections.heading: What you'll do with it
points: Create a project and pick its **project ID**, which becomes your address: `<project-id>.web.app`.
Turn on the **database** (Firestore) and **Google sign-in**, so your site can save things and let visitors sign in.
Make a **key** (a private file) that lets GitHub publish your site to Firebase for you. It goes only into a GitHub secret, never into a chat.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: The free **Spark plan** is enough for a site like this. No credit card is needed.
Firebase is part of Google, so you sign in with your Google account.

terms.meaning: Your website's home inside Firebase. Its **project ID** becomes your address, `<project-id>.web.app`, and can't be changed.
Puts your site online at that address.
A database: where your site stores things like messages.
Lets visitors sign in, for example with Google.
Rules about who can read or write your data. They start locked down.
The Firebase website where you create the project and flip these switches.
Firebase's free plan: enough for a hobby site, no credit card.

steps.title: Connect Claude to GitHub
steps.why: This lets Claude see and change your website's files.
do: Open the Claude app, tap the **Code** tab, then tap **New session**.
Above the text box, tap the chip with the GitHub logo. If GitHub isn’t connected yet, it offers to connect it (look for **Connect GitHub**). Your browser opens.
Sign in to GitHub with the account you will use for everything. If your browser is already signed in to a different GitHub account, sign it out first.
On the 'Authorize Claude' screen, tap **Authorize**.
On the install screen, under **Repository access** choose **All repositories**, then tap **Install**. (Choosing only some repositories is the most common cause of 'repository not found' later.)
Enter your GitHub password if it asks, and you are sent back to the Claude app.
steps.success: On the New session screen, a chip with the GitHub logo shows a repository name, like “my-site · main”, above the text box.

trouble.fix: Open github.com/settings/installations, tap Claude, Configure, choose All repositories, Save.

explainer.title: Connect Claude to GitHub
explainer.intro: Your website’s files will live on GitHub. Connecting lets Claude, the AI that builds your site, open those files and change them when you ask. It takes about a minute, and you only do it once.

sections.heading: You stay in charge
points: Claude works on a private copy. You check a preview before anything goes live.
You can disconnect Claude at any time in your GitHub settings.

steps.title: Create your site's repo from the starter
steps.why: Your site's files live in your own GitHub repo; every change is saved there and can be undone.
do: Open the [starter template](https://github.com/michaelbarzyk/new-website-starter) and tap **Use this template → Create a new repository** (use 'Request desktop site' if you don't see it).
Name it anything you like, for example **my-website** (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens). Choose **Private**. Tap **Create repository**.
steps.success: You land on your new repo's page, and it lists a `.claude` folder and a `CLAUDE.md`.

automation.note: Can be done by the site with GitHub's 'generate from template' API and the user's GitHub token.

trouble.symptom: You can't see the Use this template button
trouble.fix: Open your browser menu, tap **Request desktop site**, and reload.

explainer.title: Create your site’s repo
explainer.intro: A repo (short for repository) is your website’s folder on GitHub. It remembers every change, so you can always go back to an earlier version. You’ll make yours from a ready-made starter, so it already has what Claude needs.

sections.heading: Why a starter?
points: It comes with instructions for Claude, so Claude builds your site the way this guide expects.
It’s a copy: changing yours never touches the original.

sections.heading: Why private?
points: Only you, and people you invite, can see your repo’s files. Your finished website can still be public.

steps.title: Save your site brief in the repo
steps.why: Claude reads this file so it already knows your answers and doesn't ask them again.
do: Open your new repo on github.com and tap **Add file → Create new file**.
In the file name box type `.claude/site-brief.json` (typing the slash makes the folder).
Paste your site brief (use the copy button below), then tap **Commit changes**.
steps.success: The file .claude/site-brief.json shows in your repo.

trouble.fix: Fill in your site name above first, then come back.

automation.note: Can be done by the site: write the file with GitHub's contents API.

steps.title: Open your repo in Claude
do: In the Claude app, open the **Code** tab and tap **New session**.

Above the text box, tap the GitHub chip (it shows a repository name and branch) and choose your new repo. If it's missing, wait a minute and refresh, or reconnect GitHub and choose **All repositories**.
Send the message below. The first start can take a minute or two.
steps.success: Claude confirms your answers in one message instead of asking everything again.

copy.label: Copy the message
copy.value: Use the new-website skill to build me a website. My site brief is in .claude/site-brief.json.

trouble.symptom: The repo is missing from the list
trouble.fix: Wait a minute, pull down to refresh, or fully close and reopen the app. Still missing? Redo the Repository access part of the connect step.

trouble.symptom: Claude explains websites in general instead
trouble.fix: Send: Read CLAUDE.md in this repo and follow it.

steps.title: Create the Firebase project
steps.why: Firebase hosts your site, database and sign-in, free at this size.
do: Open the [Firebase console](https://console.firebase.google.com) (Firebase's control panel) and tap **Add project**.
Give the project any name you like. Under it, Firebase shows a **Project ID**. If it adds random letters, or says the name is taken, tap the pencil and edit it until you like it.
The Project ID becomes your free web address, **<project-id>.web.app**, and can **never be changed**. Pick one you'll be happy with.
Turn **Gemini in Firebase OFF** and **Google Analytics OFF** (optional extras you don't need). Accept the terms. If it offers billing or an upgrade, skip it; the free plan is enough.
When the project is created, copy its **Project ID** (Project settings shows it) and type it into the box below.
steps.success: You see the new project's overview page, and Project settings shows your Project ID.

trouble.fix: Firebase tells you straight away and suggests another. Add a short suffix (like `-1`) or try a different name until it accepts one.

trouble.symptom: The id has random letters added
trouble.fix: Tap the pencil and edit it before you tap Create; it can't be changed later.

automation.note: UNVERIFIED: Firebase management API (projects + addFirebase) with the user's Google token.

explainer.title: Create your Firebase project
explainer.intro: Firebase is Google’s free tool that hosts your website, keeps its data and handles sign-in. A project is your site’s home inside Firebase. You create it in Firebase’s own console, so Firebase itself checks that the address you want is free.

sections.heading: Why Firebase picks the address
points: Project IDs are first come, first served across all of Firebase, so common names are often taken. Firebase tells you, so you never end up with an address you can’t use.

steps.title: Create the database
do: Open [Firestore]({{firestoreUrl}}) (menu **Databases & Storage → Firestore**; older console: Build → Firestore Database) and tap **Create database**.
Choose **Standard**, location **nam5 (United States)** (where your data is stored), and **Production mode** (locked until your rules open it). Tap **Create**.
steps.success: You see an empty Firestore with a **Data** tab.

automation.note: UNVERIFIED: Firestore admin API; the API may need enabling first.

explainer.title: Create your database
explainer.intro: Firestore is Firebase’s database: where your site keeps its own information, like messages or posts. You create an empty one now, and it starts locked, so nothing can be read or written until your site’s rules say so.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: The location can’t be changed later; the United States choice is fine for most sites.
Production mode is the safe setting: it keeps everything locked until you open it on purpose.

steps.title: Turn on Google sign-in
steps.why: Sign-in is how you, the owner, log in to edit your site, and how visitors can send you messages later. Browsing stays public: nobody has to sign in to look around.
do: Open [Authentication]({{authUrl}}) (menu **Security → Authentication**; older console: Build → Authentication) and tap **Get started**.
Open **Sign-in method**, tap **Google**, and switch **Enable** on.

For the **public-facing name**, type your site's name (it shows on the Google sign-in popup). For the **support email** (the address people can write to about sign-in), pick your own email. Tap **Save**.
Leave **Anonymous** OFF (it lets people in without any account).
steps.success: Google shows as **Enabled** in the Sign-in method list.

automation.note: UNVERIFIED and probably the hardest step: enabling Google needs an OAuth client. May stay as guided taps.

explainer.title: Turn on Google sign-in
explainer.intro: Sign-in is how you, the owner, log in to edit your site. Visitors can look around without signing in. If you later add things that need to know who someone is, like sending you a message, they can sign in with their Google account too. Firebase handles the passwords, so you never touch them.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: Your site stays public: nobody has to sign in just to browse it.
The public-facing name shows on the Google sign-in popup, so type your site’s name.
Leave **Anonymous** off. It lets people in without any account, and you want to know who signed in.

steps.title: Register the web app and copy its settings
steps.why: These six values are your site's address-book entry for Firebase.
do: On **Project overview**, tap **Add app** (under the project name) and choose the web icon `</>`.
Nickname: your site's name. Leave **Firebase Hosting unchecked**. Tap **Register app**.
It asks **npm or script tag**: choose **npm** (a way of adding ready-made code to a site; Claude uses it later, so ignore the install commands).
Copy the whole **firebaseConfig** block (the code with apiKey, authDomain, projectId and the rest) and paste it into the box below. These settings are public by design, so this is safe to share.
steps.success: The box below says all six settings were found.

automation.note: UNVERIFIED: webApps.create and webApps.getConfig in the Firebase management API.

explainer.title: Connect your site to Firebase
explainer.intro: A web app is the entry inside your project that stands for your website. Registering one gives you six settings, your site’s address-book entry for Firebase. They’re public by design, so it’s safe to paste them here.

sections.heading: Why we ask for these
points: Your site needs these six settings to find your Firebase project, like an address on an envelope.
Firebase makes up three of them (a code for your site, a number and an ID), so we can’t guess them: you copy them from Firebase.
They’re public by design. What protects your site is your database rules and sign-in, not these.

steps.title: Make the deploy key (the only sensitive step)
steps.why: This key lets GitHub publish your site and rules for you.
do: Open [Service accounts]({{serviceAccountsUrl}}) (**Project settings** → **Service accounts**: a robot login for your project) and tap **Generate new private key**, then **Generate key**. A `.json` file (a plain text file) downloads to your phone.
Ignore the 'Admin SDK configuration snippet' above the button; it's example code for programmers.
Copy ALL the text in the file: open your browser's downloads list and tap the file, or use the Files app (iPhone: preview it, or Share → Save to Notes, then copy).
**Never paste this key into the Claude chat or any website.** It goes only into a GitHub secret in the next steps.
steps.success: You have the file's text copied and ready to paste in the GitHub step.

trouble.symptom: Can't open or copy the file
trouble.fix: Try the other route (browser downloads list vs Files app), or do this step on a computer.

automation.note: UNVERIFIED: IAM service-account keys API, straight to a GitHub secret. Organisations may block key creation; Workload Identity Federation avoids keys.

explainer.title: Make the deploy key
explainer.intro: The deploy key is a private file that lets GitHub publish your site to Firebase for you. It’s the one sensitive thing in this whole guide: keep it out of chats and websites. It only ever goes into a GitHub secret.

sections.heading: Why be careful
points: Anyone with this key could change your Firebase project, so treat it like a password.
You’ll delete the downloaded file once it’s saved.

steps.title: Give the key two permissions
steps.why: The key starts with few permissions. These two let it check that the database is on and publish your rules.
do: Open the [Google Cloud IAM page]({{iamUrl}}) (where permissions are set) and sign in with the same Google account. Accept any welcome screen.
Tap the pencil on the row **firebase-adminsdk-…**, then **Add another role** (a role is a set of permissions) and add **Service Usage Consumer**.
Tap **Add another role** again and add **Firebase Rules Admin** (type `rules` in the role box; if it's missing, **Firebase Admin** also works but is broader). Tap **Save**.
Keep its existing roles. Leave the **Owner (Legacy)** row (that's you) alone. Don't add any Cloud Datastore roles.
Wait 1 to 2 minutes: Google applies these slowly.
steps.success: The firebase-adminsdk row lists both new roles alongside its existing ones.

trouble.symptom: Deploy fails with `Permission denied to get service firestore.googleapis.com`
It still fails right after you added the role
trouble.fix: Wait 2 minutes and re-run the failed job.

explainer.title: Give the key two permissions
explainer.intro: A new deploy key can do very little. Two permissions let it check that your database is on and publish your site’s rules. You add them on Google Cloud, the platform Firebase runs on.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: A role is a named set of permissions. You’re giving the key two of them.
Google applies a new role slowly, so a wait of a minute or two is normal.

steps.title: Save the key as a GitHub secret
steps.why: Only GitHub's CI can use the secret; it's hidden once saved.
do: Open the [new secret page]({{secretsUrl}}). If it shows a list, pick your site's repo, then **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret** (tap 'Desktop site' if the phone view hides Settings).
Name: exactly **{{secretName}}**. Value: paste the whole key text. Tap **Add secret**.
Delete the downloaded file from your phone.
steps.success: The secret {{secretName}} shows in the repo's Actions secrets list.

trouble.symptom: The deploy later says the secret is missing or empty
trouble.fix: The name must match exactly and the value must be the whole JSON text.

automation.note: Can be done by the site: encrypt client-side and PUT the secret with the user's GitHub token.

explainer.title: Save the key as a GitHub secret
explainer.intro: A GitHub secret is a private value stored in your repo’s settings. GitHub’s automatic jobs can use it to publish your site, but nobody can read it back. This is where the deploy key finally goes.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: Once saved, a secret is hidden: you can replace it, but nobody can read it back.
The exact name matters: your site’s publishing job looks for it by name.

steps.title: Claude builds your first draft
do: Claude scaffolds your site into your repo with your real Firebase settings and owner email **{{ownerEmail}}**, then runs the format, lint, test and build checks. All must pass before moving on.
Claude opens a pull request into `main` for this first release (later changes go through `dev`). GitHub checks it and posts a private **preview link**.
steps.success: Claude shows you the preview link. Open it on your phone.

automation.note: Could run in GitHub Actions from the repo's site-brief.json, with no Claude needed for scaffolding.

steps.title: Ship it
steps.why: Nothing goes live until you say so, so you can't break your real site while experimenting.
do: Look around the preview. Tell Claude what to change in plain words (for example 'make the heading bigger').
When you're happy, tell Claude **ship it**. GitHub publishes your database rules first, then your site (about a minute).
Say **check** and Claude confirms both finished.
steps.success: Both deploy jobs show a green check, and {{liveUrl}} loads your site.

trouble.symptom: Google sign-in doesn't work on the preview link
trouble.fix: Expected: preview addresses aren't trusted for sign-in. Test it on the live address.

trouble.symptom: The rules job fails with a 403
trouble.fix: See the permission steps above and re-run after 2 minutes.

automation.note: Merge the pull request and poll check results through the GitHub API.

steps.title: Sign in and become admin
do: Open [{{liveUrl}}]({{liveUrl}}) and tap **Sign in** with **{{ownerEmail}}**.
The **Admin** link and edit buttons appear. Nothing to set up: your email is on the site's owner list, so your first sign-in makes you admin.
steps.success: You see the Admin link while signed in.

trouble.fix: Check both deploys finished, that you signed in with {{ownerEmail}} (a verified Google account), then close the tab, reopen the site and sign in again.
Firebase → Authentication → Settings → Authorized domains → add the address you're on.
